sections.heading: An explicit finite-dimensional gadget
paragraphs: Fix m≥2 and put v=2m+1. Take the vertex set Z/vZ and the m shifts σ_i(w)=w+i for i=1,...,m. The neighbours σ_i(w) and σ_i⁻¹(w), as i varies, are exactly the v−1 vertices different from w. Thus, for every function y on the vertices with sum S, the sum of y over these successors and predecessors is S−y_w. This elementary circulant identity is the only graph existence input.

Use one coordinate for each oriented edge (i,w), one link coordinate for each vertex w, and one height coordinate. Define the linear map L by edge coordinate x_i+y_w+y_{σ_i(w)}, link coordinate y_w, and height X+S, where X=Σ_i x_i and S=Σ_w y_w. The atom space is the rational range of L. Its integer points will be constrained by coordinate nonnegativity. The sum of all edge and link coordinates is v(X+S): each x_i occurs v times, each y_w occurs 2m times on edges and once as a link.

There are m cycle atoms A_i=L(e_i,0), v vertex atoms B_w=L(0,e_w), and one links atom C=L(−2·1,1). Every atom has height one and nonnegative integer coordinates. The cycle atom has ones on the edges of one colour; the vertex atom has ones on its incident edges and its own link; C has ones on all links and zeros on the edges. The identity Σ_w B_w=2Σ_i A_i+C follows coordinate by coordinate. This is the balance relation from which the exponent gap will arise.

sections.heading: Lemma: classification of nonnegative integral height-one points
paragraphs: Suppose L(x,y) is integral, nonnegative and has height one. The link coordinates show that all y_w are integers. An edge coordinate then shows that every x_i is an integer. Thus y_w≥0, X+S=1, and x_i+y_w+y_{σ_i(w)}≥0 for every i,w. Summing the last inequalities over w gives v x_i+2S≥0. Summing these colour inequalities gives vX+2mS=v−S≥0, so S≤v.

There is a second useful estimate. Fix w and sum the inequalities on both edges incident to w in every colour. Their total is 2X+2m y_w+(S−y_w)=2−S+(2m−1)y_w≥0. Consequently S≤2+(2m−1)y_w. If some y_w=0, then S≤2. If an x_i were negative, integrality would give x_i≤−1, and hence v x_i+2S≤−v+4<0 because v≥5. Therefore all x_i are nonnegative. Since X+S=1 and all variables are now nonnegative integers, exactly one of them is one and all the others are zero. This gives a cycle or vertex atom.

If no y_w is zero, then y_w≥1 for all w, hence S≥v. Together with S≤v this yields y_w=1 for every w. The edge inequalities give x_i≥−2, while X=1−v=−2m. There are m such variables, so each is −2. This gives C. We have therefore proved that the only integral, nonnegative, height-one points in the atom space are the m+v+1 atoms just described. At height zero, nonnegativity and the coordinate-sum identity force every coordinate to vanish. These are complete classifications, not assumptions about a chosen generating set.

sections.heading: Lemma: realizing exactly the allowed integer factors
paragraphs: Assign pairwise distinct small primes to the edge coordinates. Let L₀ be their product. Assign distinct link primes, each larger than L₀, and let C₀ be their product. In particular L₀<C₀. Choose a prime p above both the prescribed lower bound and 2L₀²+C₀L₀. Bertrand's postulate supplies a prime q with pL₀<q≤2pL₀. Use q as the height prime and set n=pqL₀. The inequalities imply p²<n<p³ and n<q²; also all coordinate primes differ from p and from q.

For a cycle atom let a_i be the product of its edge primes. Then 1≤a_i≤L₀, so both qa_i and pqa_i lie in {1,...,n}, while p²qa_i>n. For a vertex atom let b_w be its link prime times the product of its incident edge primes. Then L₀<b_w≤C₀L₀<p. Hence qb_w≤n but pqb_w>n. The links atom similarly corresponds to qC₀≤n, and pqC₀>n. Finally, p²<n<p³ means that the allowable pure p-powers in the interval are 1,p,p².

We claim that these are every interval factor whose p-free exponent vector lies in the atom space. For such a factor j≤n, its exponent of q is at most one because n<q². If that exponent is zero, the height-zero classification forces all its p-free coordinates to vanish; unique prime factorization makes j a pure p-power, hence 1,p or p². If the q exponent is one, the height-one classification makes its p-free part one of the cycle, vertex or links bases. The preceding upper bounds allow exactly the two p-variants of a cycle and the single variant of each vertex and the links atom. An exponent vector in the embedded atom space has no prime coordinates outside the chosen ones, so no extra prime factor has been overlooked. Unique factorization also proves that every displayed integer is distinct: equal numbers would have the same atom and p exponent.

The full allowed set is therefore {1,p,p²}, the pairs qa_i,pqa_i, the v vertex numbers qb_w, and qC₀. This is the arithmetic bridge from a rational linear construction to actual distinct factors in the complete interval.

sections.heading: Lemma: the exact two-block exponent support
paragraphs: Let T=Σ_w B_w be the target p-free vector, and let t₀ be its corresponding positive integer with no p factor. To make a selected product have p-free vector T, write d_w∈{0,1} for the selection of the vertex atom B_w, c∈{0,1} for C, and a_i,b_i∈{0,1} for the two cycle numbers qa_i and pqa_i. The link coordinates give d_w+c=1 for every w. The edge coordinates give a_i+b_i+d_w+d_{σ_i(w)}=2.

If c=0, then every d_w=1 and every a_i=b_i=0. If c=1, then every d_w=0 and every a_i=b_i=1. Thus there are exactly two structural ways to make the p-free target: choose all vertices, or choose C and both numbers of each cycle. The latter contributes exactly m extra p factors. Independently choosing p and p² contributes any exponent in {0,1,2,3}; choosing 1 has no effect on the product. Hence a subset of the allowed factors has product p^e t₀ exactly when e∈{0,1,2,3}∪{m,m+1,m+2,m+3}. Every exponent on the displayed right side is realized by the indicated choices. The equations exclude every other exponent, even when the subset omits or includes the factor 1.

sections.heading: Lemma: embedding the gadget in all of {1,...,n}
paragraphs: The preceding calculation still concerns a particular collection of factors. To prevent the other interval integers from filling a gap, let F(j) be the p-free prime-exponent vector of j. Work in the finite-dimensional rational vector space spanned by F(1),...,F(n), and the atom space A. There is a rational linear functional ℓ vanishing on A and nonzero on every F(j) outside A. Indeed, each outside vector excludes one proper hyperplane of the annihilator of A; a finite union of proper rational hyperplanes cannot fill that annihilator. Choosing outside their union gives ℓ.

Give interval factor j the rational weight w_j=ℓ(F(j)), and let W be the set of factors with positive weight. All gadget factors have weight zero. Define the baseline M=(∏_{j∈W}j)t₀. Suppose an arbitrary interval subset U has product with the same p-free vector as M. Applying ℓ gives Σ_{j∈U}w_j=Σ_{j∈W}w_j. The right side is the largest possible sum over an interval subset: it includes every positive term and no negative term. Equality therefore forces every positive factor into U and excludes every negative factor. The remaining factors have weight zero, hence have p-free vector in A by the choice of ℓ, and have already been classified as gadget factors.

Consequently U is W together with a subset of the gadget. Cancelling the baseline factors reduces its product to the exact two-block support proved above. Conversely each supported gadget subset is disjoint from W and can be adjoined to W. Thus, for every positive integer x with F(x)=F(M), membership in the complete-interval subset-product set is equivalent to x=p^e M for e∈{0,1,2,3}∪{m,m+1,m+2,m+3}. This is an exact fibre statement over the whole interval.

Finally write M=p^h d with p∤d. Unique factorization gives an arbitrary x in this fibre the form p^k d. The exact attainable exponents are h through h+3 and h+m through h+m+3. Given a prescribed positive gap length g, choose m=g+4. The g exponents h+4,...,h+g+3 are missing. The construction allows p above any prescribed bound. In particular, taking g=1 supplies two attainable endpoints surrounding a missing interpolation level. No assertion about a smallest counterexample or a uniform fixed prime is needed.

sections.heading: The factor rank and its corner formula
paragraphs: Let a Ferrers board have rows 0,...,n−1, columns 0,...,W−1 and nonincreasing row lengths ℓ_u, clipped at W. A cell (u,v) is allowed when v<ℓ_u. Let α_s be the maximum number of allowed cells in a set with at most s cells in every row and every column. Bipartite edge colouring identifies such a set with a union of s disjoint matchings. This equality concerns edge sets; it is not a statement that a chosen colouring must already have a prescribed list of colour sizes.

For a corner (i,j), let A(i,j) be the number of allowed cells with u≥i and v≥j. The corner bound is α_s≤s(i+j)+A(i,j). To prove it, partition a feasible set into cells in the first i rows, cells in the first j columns outside those rows, and cells in the remaining corner. The first two parts contribute at most si and sj and the last at most A(i,j). The Ferrers factor/min-cut theorem gives equality at some corner, hence α_s=min_{i,j}{s(i+j)+A(i,j)}. The source develops this formula through capacitated matching and actual finite cell sets, including clipped boards and empty row or column sets. We use that standard finite factor theorem below, while proving the additional equality geometry explicitly.

sections.heading: Lemma: the two ranks force a nearly square tight corner
paragraphs: Assume 1≤r≤k, 0≤e<r, α_r=rk−e, and α_{r+1}=(r+1)k−r−e. Choose a corner attaining the second minimum and, among all such corners, maximize i+j. Put A=A(i,j). The r-corner lower bound gives rk−e≤r(i+j)+A, while equality at r+1 gives (r+1)(i+j)+A=(r+1)k−r−e. Subtracting yields i+j≤k−r, and substituting back yields A≥r²−e.

Removing the first remaining row changes the (r+1)-score by r+1 minus the length of that row strip. A strip of more than r+1 would make the new score smaller than its minimum. A strip of exactly r+1 would preserve equality and increase i+j, contradicting maximality. Therefore its length is at most r. The same argument applies to the first remaining column. Ferrers nesting now puts every allowed cell of the corner in the r by r box starting at (i,j), so A≤r².

If i+j≤k−r−1, the exact (r+1)-score would give A≥r²+r+1−e>r², a contradiction. Hence i+j+r=k and A=r²−e. Since e<r, the corner contains more than r(r−1) cells. It must meet the last row and the last column of its r by r box. Ferrers downward closure then makes its first row and first column full. Separate witnesses establish these two strips; no bottom-right cell or completely filled square is claimed when e>0. The remaining corner is therefore a genuine nearly square Ferrers shape with exactly e missing cells.

sections.heading: Lemma: every prescribed optimum has the same red budget
paragraphs: Now fix any feasible r-factor F with |F|=rk−e and call its cells red. At the tight corner, the bound |F|≤r(i+j)+A is an equality. Equality in the three-part counting argument forces every first-row capacity and every first-column capacity to be saturated, forces the top-left i by j rectangle to contain no red cells, and forces all allowed cells of the nearly square corner into F. This is a conclusion about an arbitrary prescribed optimum F.

Focus on the top arm, consisting of rows u<i and columns v≥j. Each top row has exactly r red cells. The r special columns j,...,j+r−1 are allowed in every top row because the first corner row is full and the upper rows are longer. The corner already places r²−e red cells in those columns. Their total r-capacity is r². Therefore at most e red cells of the top arm lie in the special columns. All its other red cells lie in the ordinary suffix columns v≥j+r. The top-arm ordinary red mass is consequently at least ri−e. Transposition gives precisely the same conclusions for the left arm, without changing any red cell.

sections.heading: Lemma: a residual Ferrers arm contains enough full matching colours
paragraphs: We give the capacitated Hall argument responsible for preservation. Consider a general top arm with a rows, r universal special columns, and nested ordinary neighbourhoods of lengths λ_u. In each row let R_u and S_u be its red ordinary and special neighbours. Assume |R_u|+|S_u|≤r, ordinary red column degrees at most r, and Σ_u|R_u|≥ra−e. Delete all red cells from the arm. For a row subset T, write N_j(T) for the number of rows of T allowing ordinary column j, d_j(T) for its ordinary red degree, and s_j(T) for its special red degree. A nonred factor with row and column capacities r has the global cut condition
Σ_u|R_u|≤r(a−|T|)+Σ_{ordinary j} min(r,N_j(T)−d_j(T))+Σ_{special j} min(r,|T|−s_j(T)).

Here is a direct proof of that condition. Sort T by decreasing ordinary neighbourhood length. Let P be its first min(r,|T|) rows and Q its remaining rows. In an ordinary column with a red edge from Q, nestedness makes every row of P allowed. Since the full ordinary red column has at most r edges, the number of nonred allowed rows in T is at least the number of red Q edges. The latter is also at most r. Thus the ordinary residual capacities cover all ordinary red mass in Q. When a column has no red Q edge, that assertion is immediate.

For each special column j, the nonred rows in P are a subset of its nonred rows in T and number at most r. Hence |P|≤min(r,|T|−s_j(T))+s_j(P). Summing over the r special columns and using Σ_{u∈P}(|R_u|+|S_u|)≤r|P| shows that their residual capacities cover the ordinary red mass in P. Adding the two estimates covers the ordinary red mass inside T. Every row outside T contributes at most r, giving exactly the displayed global cut condition.

Capacitated Hall, equivalently integral max flow in the finite bipartite network, therefore supplies a nonred factor with at least Σ_u|R_u|≥ra−e cells and degree at most r. Properly colour its edges with r colours. Each colour is a matching of size at most a. The sum of colour deficits from a is at most e, so at most e colours can be deficient. There are at least r−e full matchings, each saturating all a rows, and they are edge disjoint. This proves the residual-arm extension lemma. The argument explains why a total budget of e special red cells loses at most e complete colours, rather than requiring each special column to be free.

sections.heading: Completing preservation and the exact rank hierarchy
paragraphs: Apply the residual-arm lemma to the top arm with a=i and to the transposed left arm with a=j. It supplies r−e matchings of size i in the top arm, and r−e matchings of size j in the left arm, all avoiding F. Match corresponding colours. Their union is still a matching: the top arm uses rows below index i and columns at least j, while the left arm uses rows at least i and columns below j. These row and column supports are separated. Each union has size i+j=k−r. Distinct unions are edge disjoint and retain every edge of the original F.

For 0≤h≤r−e, adjoin any h of these new classes to F. The result is a feasible (r+h)-factor of size rk−e+h(k−r). The same corner bounds α_{r+h} above by (r+h)(i+j)+(r²−e), which is exactly that size. Therefore α_{r+h}=(r+h)k−hr−e. For the ordinary matching rank, deleting the r corner rows leaves an empty southeast corner, so the (i+r,j) cut gives α_1≤i+r+j=k. Conversely any r-factor decomposes into r matchings, giving rk−e≤rα_1. Because e<r and α_1 is integral, α_1≥k. Thus α_1=k.

When e=0, an r-edge-colouring of the original factor has r classes of size k, because their sum is rk and no matching is larger than k. The extension supplies r additional classes of size k−r. Every prefix through 2r attains the corresponding rank. When e=1 and r≥2, the original r classes have sizes k except for one class of size k−1; order that deficient class last. The r−1 new classes have size k−r, yielding the advertised one-defect prefixes through 2r−1. For e>1 the argument preserves the total original deficit but does not impose a particular distribution among supplied colour classes. Finally, row-column nonincidence of cells is exactly independence in the Young-diagram cell graph, so the factor statements transport to the submitted independence-rank formulation.

sections.heading: Square-residue counting and the exact quotient equation
paragraphs: Let a(n) count distinct residues of squares modulo n, including zero. For an odd prime p, the nonzero squares pair the nonzero residues under x↦−x, so there are (p−1)/2 nonzero square residues and (p+1)/2 square residues in total. Chinese remaindering identifies square residues modulo a product of distinct primes with the product of their square-residue sets. Thus, for odd primes p<q<r, set a=(p+1)/2, b=(q+1)/2, c=(r+1)/2, N=pqr and R=abc; then a(N)=R.

Assume, for contradiction, R(R−1) divides N²−1. Since N>1 and R>1, there is a positive integer K with N²=KR(R−1)+1. We will first bound the finite prefix (p,q,K), without bounding the third prime directly, and then exclude every possible integer c. The residue-count bridge is essential: an arithmetic theorem about abc alone would not yet prove the OEIS statement.

sections.heading: Lemma: bounding the smallest prime and the quotient
paragraphs: Since a,b,c≥2, N=(2a−1)(2b−1)(2c−1)≤(2a−1)·4bc=8R−4bc≤8R−16, and R≥8. Therefore N²≤(8R−16)²<64R(R−1)+1. The quotient equation forces K<64, so K≤63. It also gives N²=KR²−KR+1<KR², because KR>1. Hence (N/R)²<K.

The normalized product is N/R=(2−1/a)(2−1/b)(2−1/c). Strict prime order gives a<b<c, so (2−1/a)^6<(N/R)²<K≤63. If a≥192, Bernoulli's inequality yields (2−1/a)^6=64(1−1/(2a))^6≥64(1−3/a)≥63, a contradiction. Thus a≤191 and p=2a−1≤381. This turns the smallest prime into a genuinely finite variable; no empirical search cutoff is assumed.

sections.heading: Lemma: an exact finite bound for the second prime
paragraphs: Fix p and its half-prime a. Put T=16p², B=⌊(T−1)/a²⌋, and d=T−Ba². The preceding-integer floor guarantees 1≤d≤a², even when T/a² is integral. A strict fixed-prefix estimate gives K<T/a². To check it, set u=bc, t=(2b−1)(2c−1), and s=2b+2c−1. Then 16u²−t²=s(4u+t)>28u>16u/a. Multiplying by p² gives N²<(T/a²)R(R−1). Comparing with N²=KR(R−1)+1 proves K<T/a². Since K is integral, Ka²<T and K≤B.

For the lower estimate, c≥b and the normalized quotient imply K>(p/a)²(2−1/b)^4. Bernoulli gives (2−1/b)^4=16(1−1/(2b))^4≥16(1−2/b). Clearing positive denominators yields T(b−2)<Ka²b≤Ba²b=(T−d)b. Hence db<2T. Integrality gives b≤⌊(2T−1)/d⌋ and
q≤qBound(p)=2⌊(32p²−1)/d⌋−1, where d=16p²−a²⌊(16p²−1)/a²⌋.

This bound remains finite for every p≤381. Choosing a preceding-integer floor rather than an informal limiting floor prevents a zero-denominator mistake. In the formal development positivity of d is a separate proved lemma.

sections.heading: Lemma: a narrow quotient interval and a discriminant certificate
paragraphs: For a fixed prime pair put H=pq and U=ab. Since c≥b+1, the normalized lower estimate gives K>H²(2b+1)²/[U²(b+1)²]. A sharper limiting upper estimate gives K<4H²/U². Its cleared difference is

Consequently the exact integer bounds are KLo(p,q)=⌊H²(2b+1)²/[U²(b+1)²]⌋+1 and KHi(p,q)=⌊(4H²−1)/U²⌋. The finite domain now consists of primes 2<p<q with p≤381, q≤qBound(p), and KLo≤K≤KHi. These bounds exclude the unbounded third prime from the enumeration.

Expand the quotient equation as a quadratic in the integer c. Define A=4H²−KU², E=4H²−KU and C=H²−1. It becomes Ac²−Ec+C=0. Completing the square gives (2Ac−E)²=D, where D=E²−4AC. The finite certificate lists, for each nonexceptional domain triple, an integer z≥0 with z²<D<(z+1)². Such a strict gap cannot contain an integer square, so that triple has no integer c satisfying the equation. This is stronger than checking a finite collection of third primes.

The archived certificate covers 7,973 domain leaves and has one square-discriminant exception, (p,q,K)=(3,17,31). That case is still impossible: H=51 and U=18, so reducing [H(2c−1)]²=K(Uc)(Uc−1)+1 modulo 3 gives 0=1. The contradiction does not require c to be prime. The generated Lean certificate proves coverage of the small prime list, the second-prime and quotient intervals, and each strict square gap; an external integer-square-root flag alone would not establish this interface.

sections.heading: Assembling the restricted OEIS theorem
paragraphs: The symbolic inequalities prove that any divisibility counterexample with three distinct odd primes supplies a triple in the finite domain and an integer solution of its quotient equation. The certificate and the exceptional congruence exclude every such solution. Therefore a(pqr)(a(pqr)−1) does not divide (pqr)²−1 for odd primes p<q<r. The equivalent modular assertion (pqr)²≡1 modulo a(pqr)(a(pqr)−1) is false. Since pqr is composite, the two sides of the restricted prime-characterization equivalence are both false, yielding the submitted restricted conjecture theorem.

This proof does not classify products with repeated prime factors, two-prime composites, products involving 2, or arbitrary integers. Those are outside its hypotheses. A release should attach the generated finite certificate and an executable checker, identify the complete domain formulas above, and state the exact frozen theorem endpoint. The ordinary argument is complete once the explicitly described finite certificate is included; a reader need not trust a search that simply reports no examples.

sections.heading: The finite statistical model and the collapsed fibre
paragraphs: Use visible spins s=(s₁,s₂,s₃,s₄)∈{−1,1}⁴ and one hidden spin. The data distribution is Q_ρ(s)=[1+ρs₁s₂s₃s₄]/16, where 0<|ρ|≤1. Let U denote uniform averaging over the sixteen states. For visible bias b∈R⁴, hidden bias c∈R and weights w∈R⁴, the visible model has potential f(s)=b·s+log cosh(c+w·s) and probability P(s)=exp(f(s))/Σ_x exp(f(x)). Its population log likelihood is L=Σ_s Q_ρ(s)log P(s). Additive constants in f do not change P.

At b=w=0 the model is uniform for every finite c, so the whole collapsed fibre has likelihood −log16. The data have zero moments for all nonempty spin products of degree less than four. Differentiating the finite sixteen-state likelihood at a collapsed point therefore gives zero in every parameter direction: visible-bias and weight derivatives are linear spin features, and the hidden-bias derivative is constant. Thus the fibre is stationary. This elementary stationarity is not the distinctive result. The theorem classifies precisely when it is locally maximal in all nine parameters, including highly unequal and zero weights.

sections.heading: Lemma: a quantitative likelihood penalty in Walsh coordinates
paragraphs: For a finite potential f write g=f−U[f], let τ=U[s₁s₂s₃s₄f] be its top Walsh coefficient, and let β_ij=U[s_i s_j f] be its six pair coefficients. Orthogonality of spin products gives U[g²]≥Σ_{i<j}β_ij². Because Q_ρ differs from U only in its four-spin moment,
L(f)+log16=ρτ−log U[exp(g)].

If |g(s)|≤ω, then log U[exp(g)]≥e^(−2ω)U[g²]/2. One way to prove this uniform bound is to set ψ(t)=log U[exp(tg)] for 0≤t≤1. We have ψ(0)=ψ′(0)=0 and ψ″(t)=Var_t(g), the variance under the exponential tilt. Every tilted state mass is at least e^(−2ω) times its uniform mass. Using Var_t(g)=inf_a E_t[(g−a)²] therefore gives ψ″(t)≥e^(−2ω)Var_U(g). Integrating twice yields the claimed factor one half. This finite argument requires no asymptotic Taylor remainder.

Consequently L(f)+log16≤ρτ−e^(−2ω)Σ_{i<j}β_ij²/2. The visible linear term b·s contributes to neither τ nor β_ij; it remains covered through the nonnegative total normalization penalty. This observation is what permits a bound in the complete parameter neighbourhood.

sections.heading: Lemma: finite differences dominate parity gain
paragraphs: Put h(x)=log cosh x. Suppose on [c−Σ_i|w_i|,c+Σ_i|w_i|] we have h″≥m>0 and |h⁽⁴⁾|≤M. Repeated symmetric finite differences give |τ|≤M|w₁w₂w₃w₄|. More explicitly, the four-spin Walsh coefficient of h(c+w·s) is (w₁w₂w₃w₄/16) times the integral of h⁽⁴⁾(c+Σ_iw_i t_i) over [−1,1]⁴; that cube has volume16.

The same two-variable difference identity, averaged over the other two spins, shows that β_ij has the sign of w_iw_j and |β_ij|≥m|w_iw_j|. Hence Σβ_ij²≥m²E(w), where E(w)=Σ_{i<j}w_i²w_j². Finally 6|w₁w₂w₃w₄|≤E(w). For example, adding the three squares (w₁w₂±w₃w₄)², (w₁w₃±w₂w₄)² and (w₁w₄±w₂w₃)² proves both signs of this inequality.
Combining these facts with the likelihood penalty gives

This estimate holds for signed, unequal and vanishing weights. If only one weight is nonzero then E(w)=0, and the inequality still gives nonincrease. A proof based solely on an equal-weight ray or a radial fourth-order expansion would leave these thin directions uncontrolled.

sections.heading: Proof of local maximality below the exact threshold
paragraphs: Write u=tanh²c and q=1−u>0. The derivatives are h″(c)=q and h⁽⁴⁾(c)=−2q(1−3u). Strict negativity of the coefficient in the preceding bound at the collapsed point is equivalent to |ρ||h⁽⁴⁾(c)|<3[h″(c)]², or 2|ρ||1−3u|<3(1−u). For 0<|ρ|≤1 and 0≤u<1, this is equivalent to u<(3+2|ρ|)/(3+6|ρ|). On u≤1/3 the inequality is automatically strict; on u>1/3 ordinary rearrangement gives the displayed threshold.

Assume the strict threshold at c₀. By continuity choose a small η>0 so that m=h″(c₀)−η>0, M=|h⁽⁴⁾(c₀)|+η, and |ρ|M/6<e^(−2η)m²/2. Continuity of the derivatives gives an interval around c₀ on which h″≥m and |h⁽⁴⁾|≤M. For (b,c,w) sufficiently close to (0,c₀,0), its entire hidden input interval stays inside that interval. Since the state space is finite and every centered potential is zero at the collapsed point, the same neighbourhood also has |g(s)|≤η for all states. The quantitative bound then proves L(b,c,w)≤−log16 throughout that neighbourhood. This is a local maximum in the full nine-dimensional parameter space. No unproved uniform Taylor estimate remains in this argument.

sections.heading: The converse, equality boundary and nonglobality
paragraphs: To see the sharp converse, fix c and write t=tanh c, q=1−t². Choose the ray w=εa and b=−tεa. It cancels the first-order visible potential. Expanding log cosh and the finite normalization gives zero likelihood derivatives through degree three, and the fourth-order coefficient
−q²E(a)/2+2ρq(3t²−1)a₁a₂a₃a₄.

Take a₁=a₂=a₃=1 and a₄ with sign ρ. Then E(a)=6 and the coefficient is q[(3+6|ρ|)t²−(3+2|ρ|)]. Above the threshold it is positive. Smoothness and Taylor's theorem, or the source's four repeated mean-value arguments on the explicit jets, give strict ascent for sufficiently small positive ε. Thus an exterior collapsed point is not a local maximum.

At equality the ray's fourth coefficient vanishes, so that calculation alone does not decide the boundary. Instead use the flat fibre: threshold equality implies c₀≠0, and there are c values arbitrarily close to c₀ with larger |c| and hence tanh²c above the threshold. Each such collapsed point has exactly the same likelihood as the boundary point, and each has arbitrarily nearby strict-ascent points. Every neighbourhood of the boundary therefore contains a point of higher likelihood. This proves that equality belongs to the saddle region.

Every neighbourhood of any collapsed point also contains a lower-likelihood point: set w=0 and perturb one visible bias to ε≠0. The data's one-spin mean is zero, giving L=−log16−log cosh ε<−log16. At and beyond the threshold, higher and lower points therefore occur in every neighbourhood, which is the stated parameter-saddle property. Below threshold the maxima are non-strict, because changing c along the collapsed fibre produces distinct points of exactly equal likelihood. Finally the threshold is less than one for |ρ|>0, so some finite hidden bias lies outside it and admits ascent above the common collapsed likelihood. Thus every collapsed point, including the stable local maxima, is globally suboptimal.

These conclusions give the complete finite-fibre classification: stationarity everywhere; local maximality if and only if the strict threshold holds; saddle behaviour at equality and beyond; non-strictness along the fibre; and nonglobality. The statement concerns the specified one-hidden-spin, four-visible-spin parity model and does not assert a classification of arbitrary RBMs or all stationary points.

sections.heading: An exact admissible exponent semigroup
paragraphs: Put q_t(x)=(1+x)^4−tx² and s=t−6, so q_s(x)=1+4x−sx²+4x³+x⁴. A radial polynomial R(|z|²) is a finite sum of squared absolute values of holomorphic polynomials exactly when every coefficient of R is nonnegative. Nonnegative coefficients give the explicit monomial summands. Conversely the coefficient of z^k z̄^k in any holomorphic squared-norm representation is a sum of squared coefficient magnitudes. Polynomial equality on C identifies that coefficient, even if the initial representation contains off-diagonal terms.

For 0<s≤1 the first power fails at coefficient x². The square has coefficient list [1,8,16−2s,8−8s,34+s²,8−8s,16−2s,8,1], which is nonnegative. The cube has first-half coefficients [1,12,48−3s,76−24s,99−48s+3s²,216−24s+12s²], central coefficient96−102s−s³, and the reflected first half. Thus the cube is nonnegative exactly when s³+102s≤96.

For the fifth power put h=1−s, B=q_1³+7x⁶, D=q_1+x² and E=q_1⁵−2189x¹⁰. All three have nonnegative coefficient lists. E has first half [1,20,155,580,1135,1784,3970,5000,4205,11580], central coefficient zero, and the reflected half. Direct expansion gives q_s⁵=E+5hx²(q_1²)²+10h²x⁴B+10h³x⁶q_1²+5h⁴x⁸D+(2189−70h²−5h⁴+h⁵)x¹⁰. Because0≤h≤1 every term is nonnegative. Closure under multiplication now gives every even exponent and every odd exponent at least5. The positive admissible exponents are exactly2, all n≥4, and3 when the central cubic inequality holds. In6<t≤7 the latter is924−210t+18t²−t³≥0.

sections.heading: A complete moment obstruction near t=8
paragraphs: Let6<t<8, δ=8−t, A=16−t and n>0. Assume q_t^n has nonnegative coefficients. Select coefficients whose index has parity opposite to n and form their centered moments about2n. The exact zeroth, second and fourth moments are M₀=(A^n−t^n)/2, M₂=8nA^(n−1), and M₄=[20n/A+384n(n−1)/A²]A^n+12nt^(n−1). These identities follow from the centered Euler operator evaluated at1 and−1.

These are moments of nonnegative weights, hence M₂²≤M₀M₄. The power-gap identity gives A^n−t^n≤(A−t)nA^(n−1)=2δnA^(n−1), so M₀≤δnA^n/A. Also t^(n−1)≤A^(n−1), hence M₄≤[32n/A+384n(n−1)/A²]A^n. Substitute and cancel positive quantities to obtain64A≤δ[32A+384(n−1)]. Rearranging gives t(10−t)≤12n(8−t). The coefficient/squared-norm bridge makes this a necessary condition for the unrestricted holomorphic squared-norm question. Exponent zero is explicitly excluded.

sections.heading: A fourth-root Fourier obstruction
paragraphs: On the unit circle, e^(−2iθ)q_t(e^(iθ))=F_t(θ)=16cos⁴(θ/2)−t. Nonnegative coefficients imply ∫₀^πF_t(θ)^n cos(jθ)dθ≥0 for every nonnegative integer j by Fourier extraction and symmetry. Choose j=0 for odd n and j=1 for even n; both integrands are negative nearπ.

For u=π−θ≤n^(−1/4)≤1,16sin⁴(u/2)≤u⁴≤1/n. Thus |F_t(θ)|^n≥(t−1/n)^n≥(1−1/t)t^n≥(6/7)t^n when t≥7. In the even case cosθ=−cosu≤−1/2, so both integrands are at most−(3/7)t^n on an interval of length n^(−1/4). The source bounds the positive part by the explicit Gaussian majorant A^n exp[−16nθ²/(9π²)] plus4^n. Its integral plusπ4^n is at most4A^n/√n; the remainder uses2√n≤2^n and A≥8.

Comparing the negative interval with that positive mass gives3t^n n^(1/4)≤28A^n, hence81nt^(4n)≤614656A^(4n). Taking logarithms yields log n≤4n log(A/t)+O(1). Since4log[(8+δ)/(8−δ)]=δ+O(δ³) and the moment bound already gives n≥constant/δ, every admissible positive exponent obeys δn≥(1−ε)log(1/δ) for sufficiently small δ, for any ε>0.

sections.heading: Quantitative lemmas and assembly for the matching upper bound
paragraphs: For0<k≤2N use Cauchy coefficient extraction at a saddle radius0<r≤1 satisfying Nμ(r)=k, with μ(r)=rq′(r)/q(r). Direct rational calculation gives μ′(r)=v(r)/r>0 and r/50≤v(r)≤160r on7≤t≤8. The endpoints μ(0)=0, μ(1)=2 give existence; μ(r)≤20r gives Nr≥k/20. Set H(θ)=[q(re^(iθ))/q(r)]^N e^(−ikθ). A positive real integral of H on[0,π] proves coefficient positivity.

The proved local complex-log expansion cancels its linear phase at the saddle, leaves Gaussian term−Nv(r)θ²/2, and has remainder bounded by100000Nr|θ|³ on |θ|≤1/128. Integrating on the fixed core cutoff1/20000000 supplies uniform M₀,c₀>0 and core lower bound c₀/√(Nr) for Nr≥M₀. Retaining Nr is essential at small-radius saddles.

For r≥1/8, fix α<1/4 and η>0 small enough that α+4η≤1/4. The middle-arc error is at mostπexp(−a_ηN), with a_η=coreCutoff²η⁴/(40000π⁶)>0. The near-π error is at most Cexp(−αδN)N^(−1/4), where C=1+10000π⁴. Exact modulus-deficit factorizations for the actual quartic give these estimates, retaining a deficit of αδ+(a+b²)/10000 nearπ; its sharp limiting δ coefficient is1/4. For r≤1/8, the entire outer arc error is instead at mostπexp(−Nr·coreCutoff²/π²).

Thus the complete integral in the compact range is at least c₀/√N minus the middle and quartic errors, and at small radius it is at least c₀/√(Nr) minus the edge error. Choose1/[4(1+ε)]<α<1/4. Then N≥(1+ε)log(1/δ)/δ makes each error a sufficiently small fraction of its positive core for small δ, provided the relevant scale is large.

The bounded remaining coefficient indices have uniform finite-window positivity: for fixed k the explicit sufficient estimate is N≥2k+k²11^k, uniformly on7≤t≤8. Palindromicity transfers the lower half to all0≤k≤4N; later coefficients vanish. Every sufficiently large exponent above the stated logarithmic threshold is therefore admissible. The lower and upper bounds squeeze the least positive admissible index n*(δ) to δn*(δ)/log(1/δ)→1.

sections.heading: Analytic appendix A: the actual saddle radius and variance
paragraphs: Write s=t−6∈[1,2], q(r)=1+4r−sr²+4r³+r⁴, A₁(r)=4r−2sr²+12r³+4r⁴ and A₂(r)=4r−4sr²+36r³+16r⁴. Set μ=A₁/q and V=A₂/q−μ². Direct expansion gives qA₂−A₁²=4rP, where P=1−sr+(9−s)r²+20r³+(9−s)r⁴−sr⁵+r⁶. Thus V=4rP/q² and μ′(r)=V/r for r>0.

Every lower bound needed for the saddle follows from three exact polynomial certificates: q−1=2r(2−r)+(2−s)r²+4r³+r⁴; 2P−1=(2r−1)²+10r²+40r³+2r⁴((r−1)²+6)+2(2−s)(r+r²+r⁴+r⁵); and A₁−2r=2r(1−r)²+10r³+4r⁴+2(2−s)r². All terms on their right sides are nonnegative for 0≤r≤1. Dropping negative terms in the definitions also gives q≤10, P≤40 and A₁≤20r. Consequently 1≤q≤10, 1/2≤P≤40, r/5≤μ≤20r and r/50≤V≤160r.

The function μ is continuous on [0,1], μ(0)=0, μ(1)=2, and μ′>0 on (0,1]. Therefore for every integer 0<k≤2N there is a unique 0<r≤1 satisfying Nμ(r)=k. The inequality μ≤20r implies Nr≥k/20. This lower bound on the scale is the bridge between coefficient indices and the analytic estimates; N alone is insufficient when r tends to zero.

Put f(θ)=q(re^{iθ})/q(r) and H(θ)=f(θ)^N e^{−ikθ}. Fourier extraction gives [x^k]q(x)^N=q(r)^N/(πr^k)·Re∫₀^π H(θ)dθ. The prefactor is positive. It is therefore enough to prove that this real integral is positive at the actual saddle Nμ(r)=k.

sections.heading: Analytic appendix B: a uniform complex logarithm and positive Gaussian core
paragraphs: Let u=f(θ)−1. The elementary bound |e^{ijθ}−1|≤j|θ| and q(r)≥1 give |u|≤(4r+4r²+12r³+4r⁴)|θ|≤24r|θ|. Taylor expansion of each of the four angular exponentials through second order has integral remainder at most j³|θ|³/6, because its third derivative has constant modulus j³. Summing their weighted remainders gives |u−iμθ+(A₂/q)θ²/2|≤32r|θ|³. Also |A₂/q|≤64r, so |u−iμθ|≤33rθ² on |θ|≤1/128.

On that interval |u|≤3/16<1/4, so the principal logarithm agrees with the convergent series log(1+u)=u−u²/2+Σ_{j≥3}(−1)^(j+1)u^j/j. Its tail has modulus at most |u|³/[3(1−|u|)]≤|u|³≤13,824r|θ|³. Further, |u²−(iμθ)²|/2≤(33rθ²)(44r|θ|)/2≤726r|θ|³. Combining these bounds with the 32r|θ|³ angular remainder yields log f=iμθ−Vθ²/2+R(θ), with |R(θ)|≤14,582r|θ|³≤100,000r|θ|³. This derives the exact generous bound used in the source, rather than assuming a local saddle expansion.

The saddle phase cancels: H(θ)=exp(−NVθ²/2+NR(θ)). Put S=√(Nr), v₀=1/50, v₁=160 and C=100,000. Then v₀S²≤NV≤v₁S² and |NR(θ)|≤CS²|θ|³. Fix h=1/20,000,000. The relation 4Ch=v₀ shows that throughout 0≤θ≤h, |H(θ)|≤exp(−v₀S²θ²/4), by bounding the real error CS²θ³≤v₀S²θ²/4.

Here is a fully quantitative positive-core proof. Take T=200 and require S≥max(2CT³,T/h)=1.6·10¹². On [0,T/S] the logarithmic error has modulus at most CT³/S≤1/2, so its imaginary part has cosine at least 1/2 and Re H≥0. On [0,1/S], NVθ²≤v₁ and Re(NR)≥−1/2, whence Re H≥e^(−81)/2. This interval contributes at least e^(−81)/(2S). On [T/S,h], bound a possible negative real part by the Gaussian modulus. The elementary tail inequality ∫ᵇʰe^(−cθ²)dθ≤e^(−cb²)/(cb) gives a loss at most 4e^(−v₀T²/4)/(v₀TS)=e^(−200)/S. Since e^(−200)≤e^(−81)/4, the whole core integral is at least c₀/S, where c₀=e^(−81)/4. Thus M₀=(1.6·10¹²)² suffices for the condition Nr≥M₀. These constants are deliberately conservative and their size affects only the eventual neighborhood, not the leading asymptotic constant.

sections.heading: Analytic appendix C: the exact boundary modulus identity
paragraphs: For r>0 set a=(1−r)²/(2r) and b=1+cosθ. Let δ=8−t=2−s, F=8+16a+4a²+δ, K=2+2a+b+2a(a+2)b, and J=2[a²(4a+12−2b)+4a((b−1)²+1)+b²(2+b)]. Substituting q(r)=r²F and expanding the real and imaginary parts of q(re^{iθ}) gives the exact identity 1−|f(θ)|²=2D, with D=4(2−b)(J+δK)/F². This finite polynomial identity is the Gap/AngleBridge certificate applied to cos²θ+sin²θ=1; it can also be checked by direct expansion.

For a≥0, 0≤b≤2 and δ≥0, every term of J and K is nonnegative. More precisely J−(8a+4b²)=2a²(4a+12−2b)+8a(b−1)²+2b³≥0, and K≥2. For 1/8≤r≤1 we have 0≤a≤4; for 0≤δ≤1, F≤137 and F²≤18,769. Therefore D≥(2−b)(a+b²+δ)/10,000. Its δ-independent part is at least (2−b)(a+b²)/10,000. The constants follow by substituting J≥8a+4b² and K≥2 and weakening 8/18,769 to 1/10,000.

To retain the sharp boundary coefficient, choose any 0<α<1/4 and let 0<η≤min(1,(1/4−α)/4). If a,b,δ≤η, then F≤8+21η and 4(2−b)K≥16−8η. The exact identity (16−8η)−(1/4−4η)(8+21η)²=164η+(4935/4)η²+1764η³≥0 proves 4(2−b)K/F²≥α. Also 2−b≥1. Splitting D into its spatial and δ terms gives D≥αδ+(a+b²)/10,000. At a=b=δ=0 the δ multiplier is exactly 1/4; this is the origin of the leading asymptotic threshold.

Let u=π−θ. Standard trigonometric bounds give 1+cosθ=1−cos u≥2u²/π² and 1−cosθ≥2θ²/π² for 0≤θ≤π. In particular b²≥u⁴/π⁴. If r≥1−η/2 and θ≥π−η, then a,b≤η, so |f(θ)|≤exp(−αδ−u⁴/(10,000π⁴)). The passage from D to this modulus bound uses |f|²=1−2D≤e^(−2D), followed by a nonnegative square root.

On the remaining compact outer region r≥1/8, θ≥h, if either r≤1−η/2 or u≥η, then a+b²≥η⁴/(8π⁴). The radial case follows from a≥η²/8; the angular case follows from the fourth-power bound. Combining this with 2−b≥2h²/π² gives D≥h²η⁴/(40,000π⁶)=a_η>0, and hence |f|≤e^(−a_η). The near-π rectangle and its complement now give uniform bounds for every compact-radius saddle, including r=1.

sections.heading: Analytic appendix D: small radii and the outer integral errors
paragraphs: For 0<r≤1/8 a separate algebraic certificate retains the scale r. Write c=cosθ and E=8r−16r²−16r³−16r⁵−16r⁶. The exact squared-modulus factorization is q(r)²−|q(re^{iθ})|²=(1−c)T, where T−E is the following sum of nonnegative terms: 4r²(4−s(1+c))+8r³(2−s)+8r³(2c+1)²+16r⁴c²(1+c)+64r⁴(1+c)+8r⁵(2−s)+8r⁵(2c+1)²+4r⁶(4−s(1+c))+8r⁷. Here s≤2 and −1≤c≤1 make every coefficient factor nonnegative.

Moreover E−4r=4r(1−4r−4r²−4r⁴−4r⁵)≥0 for r≤1/8, and q(r)≤2 by dropping its negative quadratic term. Thus D=(1−c)T/(2q(r)²)≥r(1−c)/2≥rθ²/π², so |f(θ)|≤exp(−rθ²/π²). On θ≥h this gives |H(θ)|≤exp(−Nrh²/π²) and a total outer loss at most πexp(−Nrh²/π²). The proof has retained Nr in both the Gaussian core and the error.

At compact radii, the middle region contributes a loss at most πe^(−a_ηN). Near π the loss is at most e^(−αδN)∫₀^ηe^(−cNu⁴)du with c=1/(10,000π⁴). Put S₄=N^(1/4) and split at 1/S₄. The first part has length at most 1/S₄. In the second part, (S₄u)⁴≥S₄u, so the integrand is bounded by e^(−cS₄u), whose integral is at most 1/(cS₄). Therefore the total loss is at most Qe^(−αδN)N^(−1/4), where Q=1+10,000π⁴. This elementary bound requires no Gamma-function integral.

The entire normalized coefficient integral is consequently at least c₀N^(−1/2)−πe^(−a_ηN)−Qe^(−αδN)N^(−1/4) for r≥1/8 and Nr≥M₀. For r≤1/8 and Nr≥M₀ it is at least c₀(Nr)^(−1/2)−πe^(−Nrh²/π²). These are the actual integrals of the polynomial, rather than a formal model with an unproved application premise.

sections.heading: Analytic appendix E: finite coefficient windows and uniform threshold assembly
paragraphs: For a fixed positive coefficient index k, write q=1+g with g=4x−sx²+4x³+x⁴. The absolute sum of the coefficients of g is at most 11. Hence every coefficient of g^j has absolute value at most 11^j; g^j has no coefficient below degree j and its degree-j coefficient is 4^j. The binomial expansion gives [x^k]q^N=binom(N,k)4^k+Σ_{j<k}binom(N,j)[x^k]g^j.

If N≥2k, all binomial coefficients in the last sum are at most binom(N,k−1). Its absolute value is therefore at most k·11^k·binom(N,k−1). The adjacent-binomial ratio is binom(N,k)/binom(N,k−1)=(N−k+1)/k. Thus the explicit sufficient condition N≥2k+k²11^k makes that ratio strictly larger than k11^k and proves coefficient positivity, uniformly in 1≤s≤2. The zeroth coefficient is always 1. For any fixed K, taking the maximum of these finite thresholds proves positivity for all k≤K.

Fix ε>0 and choose 1/[4(1+ε)]<α<1/4; then choose η as in appendix C. At N≥N_δ=(1+ε)log(1/δ)/δ, the compact quartic loss divided by its core is bounded by (Q/c₀)N^(1/4)e^(−αδN). For sufficiently small δ this function of N is decreasing throughout N≥N_δ, since its logarithmic derivative is 1/(4N)−αδ<0. At N_δ its value is a constant times log(1/δ)^(1/4)δ^(α(1+ε)−1/4), which tends to zero. This proves the required error bound uniformly for every larger exponent, not just at one chosen exponent.

The middle loss/core ratio is (π/c₀)√N e^(−a_ηN), which tends to zero. At small radii, the corresponding ratio is (π/c₀)√(Nr)e^(−Nrh²/π²), which tends to zero as Nr increases. Choose a finite scale M large enough for the positive core and this last error, and choose K>20M. For k>K the saddle relation gives Nr≥k/20>M. At compact radii N≥8M₀ suffices for the core, and the two compact errors are small by the preceding uniform estimates. For k≤K use the finite window bound. Shrinking δ ensures N_δ exceeds all fixed exponent bounds just selected.

This proves strict positivity for all lower-half coefficient indices 0≤k≤2N. The quartic is palindromic, so its Nth power is palindromic of degree 4N; replacing k by 4N−k proves every remaining coefficient positive. Coefficients above degree 4N vanish. The coefficient/squared-norm criterion now supplies the function-level holomorphic squared-norm representation. Together with the previously proved Fourier lower bound this gives the normalized least-index limit with constant one. When choosing the least integer exponent, apply the upper argument with a smaller internal ε and absorb the ceiling error δ/log(1/δ), which tends to zero.

sections.heading: The sharp residual inequality and its relation to prior work
paragraphs: Let H be a finite simple r-uniform intersecting hypergraph and let τ(H) be its minimum transversal size. The result is4τ(H)≤|H|+r+3. In particular, if τ(H)=r then |H|≥3r−3. The proof strengthens the constant4 in the finite residual inequality of Varun Sivashankar, arXiv:2606.24878v2. Its auxiliary matching and witness setup is credited to that source. The sharper asymptotic coefficient in Sivashankar’s work is a separate result and is not improved by this finite additive refinement.

We first prove the residual inequality when every vertex has degree at most3. For any edge E, intersectingness givesΣ_{F∈H}|E∩F|≥r+|H|−1, whereas the degree bound givesΣ_{v∈E}deg(v)≤3r. Thus |H|≤2r+1. This elementary edge-count bound will be used to identify the sole possible equality obstruction.

sections.heading: Good triples, witnesses and the selected-incidence inequality
paragraphs: A good triple is a set of three hyperedges sharing a vertex. In degree at most3 it is exactly the three-edge block through that vertex. Choose a maximum collection M of pairwise disjoint good triples, where disjointness concerns hyperedge indices, not disjoint hyperedges in the original intersecting hypergraph. Write t=|M|, let U be the unmatched hyperedges, and put u=|U|. Then |H|=3t+u. One vertex covers each matched triple; pairing the remaining intersecting edges covers U in at most⌈u/2⌉ vertices. Hence τ(H)≤t+⌈u/2⌉.

Maximum matching leaves no good triple entirely in U. Choose a common vertex ω({E,F}) for each pair of unmatched edges. The chosen vertices are distinct: if two different unmatched pairs had the same witness, their union would contain at least three edges at that vertex, producing a good triple in U. Every selected witness has exactly two incidences with U and at most one with the matched edges.

For each matched hyperedge p, form a link graph G_p on vertex set U: put the pair {E,F} in G_p exactly when its witness belongs to the three-edge block {E,F,p}. No pair belongs to two colour graphs. Within one matched triple {p,q,r}, every edge of G_p meets every edge of G_q, and similarly for the other two pairs of colours. Otherwise two disjoint unmatched pairs with those colours would yield two disjoint good triples replacing the one original matched triple, increasing the matching. This is an exchange argument in the auxiliary triple system.

Let S count matched/unmatched pairs whose intersection is witnessed by a selected vertex. It is at most the sum of the supports of all G_p: a selected witness of colour p contributes its two unmatched endpoints to that support. The selected vertices contribute u(u−1) incidences with U, twice the number of unmatched pairs. There are3tu matched/unmatched pairs altogether. An unselected vertex with a incidences in U and b in matched edges satisfies a+b≤3 and a≤2, so ab≤2a. Therefore unselected U incidences are at least(3tu−S)/2. Total U incidences equal ur, giving the precise inequality2u(u−1)+3tu≤2ur+S.

sections.heading: Lemma: bounds for three cross-intersecting colour graphs
paragraphs: Consider three edge-disjoint simple graphs on a common u-point ground set. Edges from different colours must intersect. Let s be the sum of their three support sizes and e the total number of edges. The elementary bounds are s≤2e, s≤max(12,u+4), and s≤max(u,12,e+4). We give the structural proof, since the refined bound is what removes the equality case.

If one colour contains two disjoint edges, let W be their four endpoints. Every edge of the other two colours lies in W, since a two-element edge meeting both disjoint pairs has one endpoint in each. If those other edges have no common vertex, every edge of the first colour also lies in W: an edge with an endpoint outside W would need its other endpoint in every edge of the other colours. All three supports then have size at most4, giving s≤12.

If the union of the other two colours has a common vertex, it has at most two edges: its other endpoints must lie in one of the fixed disjoint pairs not containing the centre. Thus their total support contribution is at most4, giving s≤u+4. Choose one of those edges as a two-point hitting set for the first colour; every first-colour edge contributes at most one new support point outside it. Hence its support is at most its edge count plus2. Adding at most twice the other two edge counts gives s≤e+4. If both other colours are empty, the first colour alone gives s≤u.

If every colour is internally intersecting, each is a star or a triangle. When every support has size at most3, s≤9. Otherwise a colour is a star with at least three distinct leaves. Every edge of another colour must contain the same centre to meet all three star edges. The whole edge union is then a single star, with at mostu−1 edges; summing the three coloured supports gives s≤e+3≤u+2. This completes all the claimed bounds, including empty colour classes.

sections.heading: The large-ground packing barrier
paragraphs: Apply the colour lemma separately to each matched triple. More generally, let a three-link packing have t blocks of three colours on a u-point ground set, with global edge disjointness. Write s_B,e_B for its block support and edge counts, S=Σ_Bs_B and E=Σ_Be_B. Global edge disjointness gives E≤u(u−1)/2.

For u≥10 the three local bounds imply us_B≤u²+4e_B. If s_B≤u+2, use s_B≤2e_B and(u−2)s_B≤u²−4. If s_B≥u+3, it is larger than12 and u, so the refined bound forces s_B≤e_B+4. Together with s_B≤u+4, this gives us_B−4e_B≤(u−4)s_B+16≤u². Summing over blocks yields uS≤tu²+4E≤tu²+2u(u−1)<u²(t+2). Hence S<u(t+2).

Only odd positive u below10 can remain. Under t+3≤u and S≥u(t+2), the old support bound S≤t max(12,u+4) reduces the possibilities to(u,t)=(5,2),(7,3),(7,4),(9,5),(9,6). The next section excludes them structurally, rather than relying on an unrecorded brute-force search.

sections.heading: The small packing cases
paragraphs: We need two elementary consequences of support saturation. If a block has s_B=2e_B, every colour graph is a matching. If e_B≥4 and u<2e_B, at least two colours are nonempty; no colour can have three disjoint edges, because a two-element edge of another colour cannot meet all three. Some colour therefore has exactly two disjoint edges and all other edges lie in their four endpoints. The whole block graph has support at most4 and e_B≤6. A saturated six-edge block is exactly K4.

On five ground points, failure of the barrier forces t=2, E=10 and S=20. Both blocks are saturated, have at most6 edges and hence have at least4 each. Their union graphs each have support at most4, but together cover all pairs of K5. That is impossible: for any vertex v, the supports containing v must cover all five vertices through pairs with v. One support of size4 is insufficient, so v must lie in both supports. Each support would contain all five vertices.

On seven points with four blocks, failure forces E=21,S=42 and saturation of every block. If all four blocks have at least4 edges, all four supports have size at most4 and cover all pairs of K7. For each vertex v let m(v) be the set of supports containing it. Every vertex lies in at least two supports, and the total memberships are at most16, so at least five vertices have exactly two memberships. Distinct such vertices have distinct membership pairs: their two supports already cover all seven vertices, and sharing a second vertex would make their union at most6. Moreover the membership pair of a twice-covered vertex is not contained in the membership set of any other vertex. There are only six pairs of four supports; at least five distinct pairs occur. Some seventh vertex has at least three memberships, excluding at least three of those pairs. Only three pairs could remain, a contradiction.

If one of the four seven-point blocks has at most3 edges, the other three must each have6 to reach21; they are saturated K4s. Two edge-disjoint K4s on seven vertices share exactly one vertex and cover the ground. No triangle can avoid both: a triangle can meet each support in at most one vertex, yet their union covers the ground. In particular a third disjoint K4 is impossible.

On seven points with three blocks, failure gives total support at least35, while each block has support at most12. Thus two blocks have support12 and the third at least11. A critical three-colour block with s>max(9,u+4) is confined to four points by the colour case analysis above. With s≥11 it has at least6 edges, so it is K4. The first two blocks are therefore K4s covering all seven vertices and sharing one vertex z. Any edge avoiding their edges must avoid z. The third block lives on the remaining six points; its support at least11 exceeds max(9,6+4), so it too is K4, contradicting the same obstruction.

On nine points the local bounds imply3s_B≤e_B+30. For s_B≤12 this follows from e_B≥s_B/2; for s_B=13 the refined bound gives e_B≥9. Summing and using E≤36 gives3S≤36+30t. Failure with t≤6 forces t=6,S=72,E=36 and equality in every local inequality. Equality and s_B≤2e_B give s_B≥12, so all six blocks have s_B=12,e_B=6. They are saturated K4s partitioning K9. In any K4 edge partition each vertex degree is divisible by3, whereas every vertex of K9 has degree8. This contradiction also excludes the nominal t=5 case. The sharp odd-ground support barrier is now proved for every required size.

sections.heading: Removing the equality obstruction and lifting by peeling
paragraphs: The baseline selected-incidence bound with S≤t max(12,u+4), together with3t+u≤2r+1, gives u+t≤r+2. Here is the short arithmetic reduction: if u+t≥r+3 then the edge-count bound forces u≥t+5. For u≥8 substitute max(12,u+4)=u+4 into the counting inequality and obtain a contradiction; the cases5≤u≤7 are immediate integer substitutions. This baseline inequality is part of the credited matching setup.

Suppose4τ(H)>|H|+r+3. If u=0, the matched cover bound already contradicts this. For positive u, combine τ(H)≤t+⌈u/2⌉ and u+t≤r+2. An even u cannot fail the desired inequality. For odd u, failure forces u+t=r+2. The degree-count bound then gives t+3≤u. Substituting r=u+t−2 into2u(u−1)+3tu≤2ur+S yields S≥u(t+2). But the actual link graphs form the packing just analyzed, whose support sum is strictly belowu(t+2), and S is at most that support sum. This contradiction proves the sharp residual inequality.

Finally remove the degree-at-most3 restriction by induction on the number of hyperedges. If a vertex has degree d≥4, delete all edges through it to obtain H′. A minimum cover of H′ together with that vertex covers H, so τ(H)≤τ(H′)+1. Uniformity and intersectingness pass to H′, and |H|=|H′|+d. The inductive bound gives4τ(H)≤|H′|+r+3+4≤|H|+r+3. If no such vertex exists, the residual theorem applies. Substituting τ(H)=r gives3r≤|H|+3.

The additive constant3 is sharp for the residual inequality: the three edges of a triangle form an intersecting2-uniform hypergraph with τ=2, and4τ=8=3+2+3. Sharpness of this residual constant should not be confused with equality examples for the bound g(r)≥3r−3 at every rank. sections.heading: The exact arithmetic fiber and the theorem proved
paragraphs: Write σ(k) for the sum of the positive divisors of k, and let F(n)=#{k≥1:kσ(k)=n}. For n≥1 every member of this fiber satisfies k≤n, so this is also the canonical bounded count #{k≤n:kσ(k)=n}. Put C=log(2539/1000)/3+log(10/9)/2, with natural logarithms. The result proved here is: for every ε>0 there is N(ε) such that, for every integer n≥N(ε), F(n)≤exp((C+ε)log n/log log n). The quantifier is uniform in all n. The exact inequality (2539/1000)²(10/9)³<9 implies C<log(3)/3. In particular this improves the positive constant in the familiar powerful-core upper bound. It does not give F(n)=exp(o(log n/log log n)), which would require that every positive constant can be used.

The proof has three independent bridges. First the arithmetic fiber injects into exponent patterns of powerful cores. Second a weighted finite count controls those patterns with an exact rational inequality. Third a moving prime cutoff removes the small-prime and rounding errors. We give the bridges explicitly so that the final asymptotic statement is not resting on an unproved finite-counting hypothesis.

sections.heading: Lemma 1: squarefree injectivity and the powerful-core injection
paragraphs: For a squarefree integer s, multiplicativity gives sσ(s)=∏_{p|s}p(p+1). These products determine their prime supports. Indeed, let p>3 be the largest prime in the union of two supports with equal products. Divisibility by p forces a factor q(q+1) on each side with q≤p. If p divides q then q=p. If p divides q+1 and q<p, then q+1≤p, hence q=p−1. This is impossible for primes p>3: p is odd, so p−1 is an even integer greater than two. Thus p occurs on both sides. Cancel its positive factor p(p+1), and continue inductively. When only 2 and 3 remain, the four possible products are 1, 6, 12 and 72; they are distinct. Consequently s↦sσ(s) is injective on squarefree positive integers.

Factor k uniquely as k=P(k)s(k), where P(k)=∏_{v_p(k)≥2}p^{v_p(k)} and s(k) is the product of the primes occurring to exponent exactly one. The factors P(k) and s(k) are coprime; s(k) is squarefree. The divisor-sum function is multiplicative on coprime arguments, so kσ(k)=P(k)σ(P(k))·s(k)σ(s(k)). If two members of the same fiber have the same core P, cancellation of Pσ(P) leaves equal squarefree products, and the preceding lemma gives equal residuals. Thus k↦P(k) is injective on a fixed fiber.

If n=∏p^{a_p}, then k divides n and each exponent of its powerful core belongs to {0}∪{2,…,a_p}. Also σ(k)≥k, so k²≤n and therefore P(k)²≤n. In logarithmic form every core pattern e=(e_p) satisfies ∑e_p log p≤(log n)/2. The image of the fiber need not be all patterns satisfying these conditions. Counting all admissible patterns gives an upper bound, and the formal source also proves equality between the fiber count and the actual image of the core map. No surjectivity onto the larger majorant is required.

sections.heading: Lemma 2: an exact weighted local inequality
paragraphs: For a≥1 set L_a(x)=1+∑_{j=2}^a x^j, where an empty sum is zero. Put x=9/10 and B=2539/1000. The crucial exact estimate is L_a(x)³≤B^a for every a≥1. The cases a=1 and a=2 are direct rational calculations. For a=3, L_3(x)=1+x²+x³=B, so equality holds. The remaining initial calculation is L_4(x)³≤B⁴, again an inequality between rational numbers.

To prove every larger exponent at once, observe that for a≥3, L_a(x)≥B and x^{a+1}≤x⁴. Since L_{a+1}(x)=L_a(x)+x^{a+1}, these two inequalities give B L_{a+1}(x)≤L_a(x)(B+x⁴)=L_a(x)L_4(x). Cubing, applying the induction hypothesis and the a=4 calculation, and cancelling B³ gives L_{a+1}(x)³≤B^{a+1}. This is a uniform argument over all exponents; it is not a numerical search over a selected exponent range.

More generally, let S be a finite set of exponent patterns satisfying e_p∈{0}∪{2,…,a_p} and ∑e_p≤m. Since 0<x≤1, each term x^{∑e_p} is at least x^m. Summing and then enlarging S to the full product of coordinate choices gives |S|x^m≤∏_p L_{a_p}(x). Cubing and using the local estimate yields |S|³x^{3m}≤B^{∑a_p}. This elementary weighted count is the finite source of the improved constant.

sections.heading: Lemma 3: the finite prime-cutoff bound
paragraphs: Fix n≥2 and a real y>1. Separate target primes p≤y from p>y. The small-prime coordinates are counted without a weight: the set {0}∪{2,…,a_p} has exactly a_p members, including when a_p=1. Write Q=∏_{p≤y, p|n}a_p and S=∑_{p>y, p|n}a_p. On the large-prime coordinates the core budget gives ∑_{p>y}e_p≤log n/(2log y). Set m=ceil(log n/(2log y)). Apply the weighted count to those coordinates and the unweighted product to the others. The resulting finite inequality is F(n)³x^{3m}≤Q³B^S.

The target factorization gives S log y≤∑a_p log p=log n. Hence S≤R=log n/log y. Moreover m≤R/2+1. Taking logarithms of the positive upper bound, with the case F(n)=0 immediate, gives log F(n)≤log Q+(log B/3−log x/2)R−log x. The coefficient is precisely C, and the last term is D=log(10/9).

No prime number theorem is needed to estimate Q. There are at most y distinct positive integers p≤y, and every target exponent satisfies a_p≤log n/log 2. Thus log Q≤y log(1+log n/log 2). We obtain the unconditional finite estimate F(n)≤exp(y log(1+log n/log 2)+C log n/log y+D). It is valid for every n≥2 and every real y>1. In the formal chain, SigmaFiberEntropy proves this estimate on the actual arithmetic fiber before SigmaFiberAsymptotic calls the analytic bridge.

sections.heading: The cutoff asymptotics and the strict improvement
paragraphs: Put L=log n and choose y=L/(log L)³ once L is sufficiently large. Then y>1 and log y=log L−3log log L. Since log log L/log L tends to zero, (log L)/(log y) tends to one. Normalize the exponent in the finite estimate by L/log L. Its large-prime term tends to C. Its small-prime term becomes log(1+L/log 2)/(log L)² and tends to zero: the numerator differs from log L by a bounded quantity, while the denominator is quadratic in log L. Its rounding term becomes D log L/L and also tends to zero. The normalized total therefore tends to C.

For every ε>0 this convergence makes the finite exponent at most (C+ε)L/log L beyond a threshold, which proves the theorem for all sufficiently large integers n. Finally, 6C=log(B²(10/9)³)<log 9=2log 3. Division by six gives C<log 3/3. This comparison uses exact rational arithmetic inside the logarithm, rather than rounded decimal constants. The structural injection and the cutoff method should be distinguished from the particular weighted improvement when crediting earlier literature.

sections.heading: The representation count and its precise scope
paragraphs: Let R(n)=#{(x,y)∈ℕ²:x³+y³=n}, where the pairs are ordered and zero coordinates are allowed. The claimed improvement is that, for every ε>0, R(n)≤exp((log(5/3)+ε)log n/log log n) for every sufficiently large integer n. This is a pointwise bound over all targets, including targets with repeated prime factors. It is a positive-constant upper bound, rather than the n^{o(1)} or boundedness conclusions appearing in stronger versions of the representation problem. The proof first treats positive primitive pairs and then restores the common divisor and zero-coordinate cases.

The arithmetic encoding into modular cubic roots follows an established coding approach. The contribution described here is the explicit weighted ternary Elias estimate, its finite 500-coordinate certificate, and the complete transfer back to the canonical all-target count. The proposed coefficient log(5/3) is about 0.510826. A bound proved only for cube-free targets has different quantifiers and does not by itself settle this all-target statement. Any claim of priority should be checked against that distinction and the full literature, rather than only compared by decimal coefficients.

sections.heading: Lemma 1: primitive solutions form a separated weighted ternary code
paragraphs: Suppose x,y>0, gcd(x,y)=1 and x³+y³=n. Then x and y are each coprime to n: a prime dividing x and n would divide y³, hence y, contradicting primitivity. For every full prime power p^a dividing n, the unit r_p=−x/y modulo p^a satisfies r_p³=1. There are at most three such units. For odd p the unit group modulo p^a is cyclic, so the kernel of the cubing map has at most three elements, including when p=3. For p=2 the unit group has order a power of two; cubing is an automorphism because three is coprime to that order. Thus its only cube root of one is one. Label the available roots independently by symbols in the three-element alphabet ℤ/3ℤ.

Give the coordinate p weight w_p=a log p. Its total weight is W=log n. Consider two distinct positive primitive solutions (x,y) and (u,v). Their integer determinant D=xv−uy is nonzero. Indeed, D=0 would give equal reduced positive fractions x/y=u/v, which forces x=u and y=v. Each coordinate product xv and uy has cube strictly less than n² because every positive coordinate has cube less than n. Positivity therefore gives |D|³<n²: the absolute difference of two nonnegative products is at most their larger product.

If two codewords agree at p, their modular ratios agree, and multiplication by the invertible denominators gives p^a|D. The agreeing full prime powers are pairwise coprime, so their product A divides |D|. Consequently A³<n² and log A<(2/3)log n. The sum of the weights of the disagreeing coordinates is W−log A>W/3. This also proves that the encoding is injective. Thus actual primitive solutions, rather than hypothetical modular data, form a weighted ternary code with strict distance greater than one third of the total weight.

sections.heading: Lemma 2: a weighted radius-19/100 ball contains at most 45 separated words
paragraphs: For a ternary word z, write d_w(z,0)=∑_{i:z_i≠0}w_i. Let a code C of size M lie in the ball d_w(z,0)≤αW, where 0≤α≤2/3. At coordinate i let n_0,n_1,n_2 be the symbol counts and t=n_1+n_2. The number of ordered mismatches at that coordinate is M²−n_0²−n_1²−n_2². Since n_0=M−t and n_1²+n_2²≥t²/2, this is at most 2Mt−(3/2)t². Completing the square around t=αM gives the affine tangent bound (2−3α)Mt+(3/2)α²M².

Sum these bounds with the nonnegative coordinate weights. The ball condition gives ∑_i w_i t_i=∑_{z∈C}d_w(z,0)≤MαW. Since 2−3α≥0, the total ordered pair distance is at most (2α−(3/2)α²)M²W. Separation, including the diagonal correction, gives the lower bound M(M−1)W/3. At α=19/100 the upper coefficient is 6517/20000. Therefore (M²−M)/3≤(6517/20000)M², equivalently (449/20000)M²≤M. If M>0, then M≤20000/449<45; the stated safe integer bound M≤45 follows. Keeping the factor 1/3 on the diagonal correction is essential to this computation.

Let B be the full weighted ball of radius 19W/100 in the ambient group (ℤ/3ℤ)^s. For each z, consider pairs (c,b)∈C×B with c+b=z. Projection to b is injective on this fiber, and translation preserves weighted coordinate mismatch. Hence the b-projections are a separated code in B and the fiber has at most 45 elements. Double-counting over all 3^s values of z yields |C||B|≤45·3^s. This argument accommodates arbitrary nonnegative weights; equal weights are not assumed.

sections.heading: Lemma 3: a uniform ball volume and the exact 500/90 bridge
paragraphs: Choose uniformly a t-element subset I of the s coordinates. The sum of its weights has average tW/s, because each coordinate occurs in exactly binom(s−1,t−1) subsets. Markov counting shows that at least (1−100t/(19s))binom(s,t) of those supports have total weight at most 19W/100, provided 100t<19s. Every such support gives 2^t words in the ball, by assigning either nonzero symbol at each support coordinate. Distinct supports give disjoint sets of words. Thus (19s−100t)binom(s,t)2^t≤19s|B|.

Put m=floor(s/500) and t=90m. Then 500m≤s<500m+500 and 19s−100t≥s. A blockwise choice of 90 positions in each of m disjoint 500-position blocks proves binom(s,90m)≥binom(500,90)^m. The ball-volume inequality therefore gives [binom(500,90)2^90]^m≤19|B|. Combine it with packing to obtain |C|[binom(500,90)2^90]^m≤855·3^s.

The exact finite certificate is 3^500≤(5/3)^500 binom(500,90)2^90. After clearing denominators it is simply the integer inequality 9^500≤5^500 binom(500,90)2^90. This can be checked with integer arithmetic, and the source proves it by exact rational normalization. Raising it to m and using s≤500m+500 gives 3^s≤3^500(5/3)^{500m}[binom(500,90)2^90]^m. Cancelling the positive block factor proves |C|≤855·3^500(5/3)^s. The zero-coordinate ambient cube has one word and is covered separately by the same constant. Applied to the preceding arithmetic code, this bounds the primitive positive count by a constant times (5/3)^{ω(n)}.

sections.heading: Lemma 4: restore all common divisors through an exact Euler product
paragraphs: Every positive representation has a unique common divisor d=gcd(x,y). Writing x=du and y=dv produces a primitive positive representation of n/d³, and necessarily d³|n. Conversely every such primitive representation scales back uniquely. Therefore the positive ordered count is exactly the sum over d³|n of the primitive counts of n/d³. This bridge is needed because the theorem is not restricted to cube-free targets.

Write B_0=5/3 and n=∏p^{a_p}. The weight B_0^{ω(n/d³)} factors coordinatewise. If d has exponent j at p, with 0≤j≤floor(a_p/3), the local contribution is one when 3j=a_p and B_0 otherwise. The sum of all local contributions is H(a)=floor(a/3)B_0+(1 if a≡0 mod 3, otherwise B_0). Hence the weighted divisor sum is at most ∏_{p|n}H(a_p). In fact the ordinary exponent parametrization gives equality; the formal upper-bound proof only needs injection of divisor exponent coordinates.

For every a≥0, H(a)≤B_0^a and H(a)≤2(a+1). The first estimate has direct cases a=0,1,2; for larger a use H(a+3)=H(a)+B_0, H(a)≥1 and 1+B_0≤B_0³. Induction in steps of three then gives H(a+3)≤H(a)B_0³≤B_0^{a+3}. The linear bound follows directly from the formula. The source uses the harmless primitive prefactor max(1,ω(n))3^507, since 855·3^500≤3^507. It obtains R_+(n)≤max(1,ω(n))3^507∏H(a_p), where R_+ counts only positive coordinates.

sections.heading: The all-target cutoff and zero-coordinate completion
paragraphs: Set U=1+log n/log 2 and fix a real cutoff y>1. There are at most y target primes p≤y, and each a_p≤log n/log 2. For these primes the linear estimate gives log H(a_p)≤log(2U)≤2log U, because n≥2 implies U≥2. For primes p>y, the exponential estimate and ∑_{p>y}a_p≤log n/log y give ∑log H(a_p)≤log(5/3)log n/log y. The prefactor max(1,ω(n)) is at most U, and log U≤y log U. Consequently R_+(n)≤exp(3y log U+log(5/3)log n/log y+507log 3).

Choose y=L/(log L)³ with L=log n. Divide the exponent by L/log L. The small-prime contribution tends to zero; the cutoff ratio log L/log y tends to one; and the constant term tends to zero. Thus, for every ε>0, R_+(n)≤exp((log(5/3)+ε)log n/log log n) for all sufficiently large n. There are at most two representations with a zero coordinate, namely (0,a) and (a,0) when n=a³. Apply the positive estimate with ε/2 and absorb this bounded addition into the remaining ε/2 margin, whose exponential grows without bound. This proves the stated bound on R(n).

The final canonical-count bridge observes that the map (x,y)↦(x³,y³) is injective, so counting pairs of cube values and counting pairs of their nonnegative roots give exactly the same number. The manuscript therefore reaches the originally defined representation function, not just an intermediate code cardinality. sections.heading: The optimized ordinary theorem: coefficient 0.4695030882…
paragraphs: The entrant-supplied ordinary exposition proves a stronger coefficient than the rational formal endpoint. Put a=(2−√2)/3, H(t)=−t log t−(1−t)log(1−t), and C_*=log3−H(a)−a log2=0.46950308823856934…. The ordinary theorem is that for every ε>0, R(n)≤exp((C_*+ε)log n/log log n) for all sufficiently large n. The submitted Lean theorem remains the weaker coefficient log(5/3). The following optimization explains the stronger ordinary result without attributing its verification to Lean.

For any fixed 0<α<a, the preceding localized average-distance calculation yields M(M−1)/3≤(2α−(3/2)α²)M². Its denominator 1−6α+(9/2)α² is positive, so M≤K_α=[1−6α+(9/2)α²]^{-1}; increasing K_α to an integer gives a harmless safe fiber bound. Double-counting translated ball incidences therefore gives |C|V(αW)≤K_α 3^s, uniformly in every choice of weights.

Fix 0<β<α and take t=floor(βs). The same first-moment support count gives V(αW)≥(1−t/(αs))binom(s,t)2^t. Its prefactor is bounded below by the positive constant 1−β/α. Stirling’s formula gives log binom(s,floor(βs))=H(β)s+O(log(s+1)), with constants depending only on β. Thus for every η>0 there is K_{α,β,η}, independent of s and of the coordinate weights, such that |C|≤K_{α,β,η}exp((log3−H(β)−βlog2+η)s). The zero-coordinate and finitely many small-coordinate cases can be absorbed in that one constant.

The function H(t)+t log2 is increasing for 0<t<2/3, since its derivative is log(2(1−t)/t). First choose β<α<a close enough to a, and then choose η>0 small enough. For every B>exp(C_*) the preceding estimate consequently gives P(n)≤K_B B^{ω(n)}, with one constant K_B independent of the target. This order of choices is what makes the arithmetic transfer uniform. The coefficient is approached from above; no estimate is asserted at a radius whose localized denominator vanishes.

Choose exp(C_*)<B<2. We may also ensure B>3/2. To see the latter threshold lies below exp(C_*), note a<1/5 and the monotonicity just established. Hence C_*>log3−H(1/5)−(1/5)log2. Exponentiating five times reduces comparison with log(3/2) to the exact inequality 3^5(1/5)(4/5)^4/2>(3/2)^5. Thus B³≥B+1 and B³≥2, which are the only local-factor inequalities required.

The gcd decomposition now gives R_+(n)≤K_B∑_{d³|n}B^{ω(n/d³)}. The local factor for exponent e=3q+r is qB+1 if r=0, and (q+1)B otherwise. It is at most B^e and at most 2(e+1). For the exponential bound check e=0,1,2,3 directly; when e≥1 the factor is at least B and T_{e+3}=T_e+B≤2T_e≤B³T_e. The e=0 to e=3 step uses B+1≤B³. These inequalities prove the all-exponent claim by induction.

The same elementary prime cutoff then bounds the logarithm of this Euler product by (log B+o(1))log n/log log n; log K_B is negligible. The small-prime part uses only the number of integers up to y and the linear local bound, with y=log n/(log log n)³. Let B decrease to exp(C_*), and absorb the at most two zero-coordinate representations. This proves the stronger ordinary theorem. It continues to leave the original polylogarithmic target open.
